case_name: Ramdas Bhikaji Chaudhari v Sada Nand & Ors.
facts: The respondents were convicted u/s. 16 (1) (a) (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and sentenced to 6 months' R.I. and fined Rupees 2,000 as modified by the Sessions Judge in appeal.

In the first place the decision of this Court in Rajal Das Guru Namal Pamanani v. State of Maharashtra 1974 Indlaw SC 55 was reconsidered by a larger Bench of 5 Judges who overruled the aforesaid decision in the case of State of Kerala v. Alasserry Mahommed 1978 Indlaw SC 330, and held that Rule 22 was purely directory and must always be construed to have been so.
The High Court accepted all the facts proved in the case and found that the confectionery drops sold by the accused to the Food Inspector by way of sample contained coal tar dye.
issues: Whether the acquittal of the respondents was legally erroneous
petitioner_arguments: In the first place he submitted that as at the time when the respondents were acquitted the previous decision of the Court reported in Rajal Das Guru Namal Pamanani v. State of Maharashtra 1974 Indlaw SC 55 held the field, it is not a fit case where we should exercise our discretionary powers u/art. 136 to set aside the order of acquittal particularly when the case was launched against the respondents as far back as 1971.

Secondly it was contended that even though the previous decision of this Court was overruled by this Court in the case of State of Kerala v. Alassery Mohammed 1978 Indlaw SC 330, yet the previous decision was the law laid down by this Court u/art. 141 of the Constitution and, therefore, the judgment of the High Court was correct
respondent_arguments: Learned counsel appearing for the respondents raised three points before us.
court_reasoning: The later decision of this Court in State of Kerala v. Alassery Mohammed 1978 Indlaw SC 330 has clearly decided the point of law against the view taken by the High Court and as a logical consequence thereof the acquittal of the respondents was wrong on a point, of law.

In similar situations in the case of the State of Bihar v. Hiralal Kejriwal [(I960) 1 S C R 726=A I R 1960 S C 47.1959 Indlaw SC 106] this Court refused to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction u/art. 136 of the Constitution and did not order the continuance of the criminal proceeding any further.
holding: We hold that the judgment of the High Court is vitiated by clear error of law and cannot be sustained.

We would allow this appeal and set aside the order of the High Court and convict the respondents u/s. 16 (1) (a) (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and sentence the respondents to fine of Rupees 2,000 each, in default 6 months' R.I.
